### Reviewer 4

Wu, Wen, Zhu et al.‘s manuscript “Critical roles of endogenous VEGF signaling for cell fate decision in human embryonic
stem cells” digs into the well explored space of signal transduction within human pluripotency to evaluate the potential role
for VEGF signaling factors to support self-renewal and block differentiation. Beginning with a somewhat simple screen, the
authors first test several less explored RTK pathways for their ability to impact “primed” state hESC self-renewal, and find a
convincing effect with the VEGFR inhibitor Axitinib. After confirming that this effect conforms with the endogenous
expression of VEGF receptors and ligands within primed state cells, the authors then thoroughly validate the role of VEGF
signaling in promoting self-renewal within this state using multiple independent small molecule inhibitors, the induction of
soluble VEGF receptors (which presumably compete for active ligand), and bulk induction of VEGFR1 and 2 targeting
sgRNAs. They then utilize combinations of small molecule inhibitors and their soluble receptor induction system to
demonstrate how VEGF signaling first supports NANOG expression which, upon destabilization, triggers BMP-supported
spontaneous differentiation towards a trophoblast stem cell-like state (which they confirm via marker-based analyses such
as IF, FACs, RT-qPCR alongside limited epigenetic analysis of the ELF5 promoter). Finally, the authors demonstrate that
VEGF related genes are only induced upon the transition from naïve to primed state pluripotency, and apply this concept to
replace the conventional 5i/L/A condition with a limited VEGF-inhibitor-based “2i/L” condition that eliminates the historically
problematic MEK1 inhibitor PD0325901 with minimal, if not improved, effects on genomic integrity and self-renewal.
Overall, I think this is a thorough, mature and compelling work, with multiple validations for each experimental observation.
The authors offer an overall coherent framework from the initial observation that VEGF signaling appears to specifically
impact primed state pluripotency, through the dissection of the genetic pathway from VEGF to NANOG to BMP-based
induction of “trophoblast-like cells,” and to the developmental induction of this pathway as part of the naïve to primed
transition. However, there are several areas where I feel that the results or interpretation of the results are overstated,
sometimes critically so. Moreover, a detailed connection for precisely how VEGF signaling might interact with the
pluripotency network (through which arm of its many downstream effectors) is not explored, but needs to be discussed more
thoroughly in the discussion. I feel that this is particularly important given the authors claims related to the potential of VEGF
inhibition to act as a substitute for the more conventional MEK1 inhibitor. A paragraph in the discussion highlighting how
VEGF may interact with more conventional signaling pathway components would provide important context.
Below are the areas that I think are the most problematic in terms of language and interpretation, as well as proposed
solutions for making sure this very interesting study is clearly communicated to the field.
In particular, the reported differentiation of primed state hESCs into bona fide TSCs is still controversial, as this would
represent a bona fide transdifferentiation event that includes global rewiring of the epigenome. As such, it would not conform
with the developmental dynamics of the early epiblast in vivo. Instead, BMP or CDX2 induction of primed state cells seems to
create a complex hybrid, possibly amniotic state that still fits many of the somewhat limited criteria tested by the authors for
a trophoblast-like identity (see in particular PMID: 33831365 as well as PMID: 21816365). My suggestion is that the authors
consider the pre-existing literature carefully when developing and explaining their model. To me, they must either use the
incorporated data and criteria from these previously papers to show more completely that their cell types resemble more
conventional hTSCs compared to primed state derived amnion-like cells or they must substantially revise this section of the
manuscript to highlight these prior works. They must make it clear that VEGF blocked primed state pluripotent cells from
spontaneous differentiation as driven by BMP4 and discuss how this triggers the induction of a trophoblast-like state that
may be more equivalent to early amnion, but remove statements or results intended to validate the equivalence of these
cells to bona fide TSCs. To me, it is a perfectly interesting and sufficient finding on its own without the added utility of being
suitable as a model for trophoblast or placental development.
The authors have done a convincing job of showing that VEGF signaling is upstream of NANOG, and that BMP4-based
differentiation is downstream. However, the OE/rescue experiments they have conducted are more similar to an “epistasis”
test (establishing the genetic order of events) than they are about direct or functional connections. The observation that
NANOG binds some BMP-associated effectors is interesting, but derived from previously generated/public data and does
not prove that NANOG is directly suppressing these targets. The language (and subheader) related to the section “NANOG
directly suppresses expression of genes associated with the BMP pathway and trophoblast lineage in primed hESCs”
should be revised accordingly to better utilize wording related to who is acting upstream to stabilize NANOG expression
(VEGF) or downstream to support spontaneous differentiation (BMP4). The observation that NANOG appears to bind some
of these promoters can be noted and the authors can suggest that this might suggest that NANOG plays dual activating and
inhibitory roles, but anything beyond that is speculation not present in the data.
The novel “2i/L” experiments are interesting but overall represent a shallow validation. I think this is fine for a wide-ranging
investigation of VEGF signaling in human pluripotent stem cells, but the authors should consider if it is worth adding
additional validation to bolster their claim, including testing additional stem cell lines, evaluating their functional potential
according to the conventions used for the publication of these prior conditions, and more carefully evaluating the effects of
this condition on long term genetic and epigenetic stability. I fully realize that such an investigation is well outside the scope
of this study. If they elect to proceed with the validation they have already done, the authors should revise their language to
highlight that their 2i/L condition offers intriguing preliminary results for simpler and more stable naïve hPSC culture
conditions, but that further work would be necessary to establish that these conditions are sufficient to capture the
complexities of self-renewal and differentiation potential long term.
I think the statement on Page 19, Line 28 reading “The finding that the uterine fluid from women with unexplained infertility
contains decreased VEGFA levels further implicates a crucial role of VEGF signaling in early human embryonic
development” should be removed. The observations or interpretations of this sort of clinical study are much more likely about
placentation rather than the differentiation of the epiblast (which the authors have already stated is an endogenous signaling
relationship).
The fact that the SHhES8 hESC line is female needs to be stated clearly in the text before presenting data related to Xist
and MeCP2 methylation in Figure 7.
The title could be revised to something more specific, such as “VEGF signaling supports primed-state human embryonic
stem cell self-renewal” or “Endogenous VEGF signaling blocks spontaneous BMP4-based differentiation in primed state
human embryonic stem cells.”

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
To answer the question more clearly, I divided Reviewer #4 comments into 7
questions below.
Comment 1: Wu, Wen, Zhu et al.‘s manuscript “Critical roles of endogenous
VEGF signaling for cell fate decision in human embryonic stem cells” digs into
the well explored space of signal transduction within human pluripotency to
evaluate the potential role for VEGF signaling factors to support self-renewal
and block differentiation. Beginning with a somewhat simple screen, the authors
first test several less explored RTK pathways for their ability to impact “primed”
state hESC self-renewal, and find a convincing effect with the VEGFR inhibitor
Axitinib. After confirming that this effect conforms with the endogenous
29
expression of VEGF receptors and ligands within primed state cells, the authors
then thoroughly validate the role of VEGF signaling in promoting self-renewal
within this state using multiple independent small molecule inhibitors, the
induction of soluble VEGF receptors (which presumably compete for active
ligand), and bulk induction of VEGFR1 and 2 targeting sgRNAs. They then
utilize combinations of small molecule inhibitors and their soluble receptor
induction system to demonstrate how VEGF signaling first supports NANOG
expression which, upon destabilization, triggers BMP-supported spontaneous
differentiation towards a trophoblast stem cell-like state (which they confirm via
marker-based analyses such as IF, FACs, RT-qPCR alongside limited
epigenetic analysis of the ELF5 promoter). Finally, the authors demonstrate that
VEGF related genes are only induced upon the transition from naïve to primed
state pluripotency, and apply this concept to replace the conventional 5i/L/A
condition with a limited VEGF-inhibitor-based “2i/L” condition that eliminates the
historically problematic MEK1 inhibitor PD0325901 with minimal, if not
improved, effects on genomic integrity and self-renewal.
Overall, I think this is a thorough, mature and compelling work, with multiple
validations for each experimental observation. The authors offer an overall
coherent framework from the initial observation that VEGF signaling appears to
specifically impact primed state pluripotency, through the dissection of the
genetic pathway from VEGF to NANOG to BMP-based induction of
“trophoblast-like cells,” and to the developmental induction of this pathway as
part of the naïve to primed transition. However, there are several areas where
I feel that the results or interpretation of the results are overstated, sometimes
critically so. Moreover, a detailed connection for precisely how VEGF signaling
might interact with the pluripotency network (through which arm of its many
downstream effectors) is not explored, but needs to be discussed more
thoroughly in the discussion. I feel that this is particularly important given the
authors claims related to the potential of VEGF inhibition to act as a substitute
for the more conventional MEK1 inhibitor. A paragraph in the discussion
30
highlighting how VEGF may interact with more conventional signaling pathway
components would provide important context.
Response to comment 1: We sincerely appreciate your thorough evaluation
of our manuscript and constructive advice. As suggested, paragraphs
discussing how VEGF signaling might link to the known pluripotency network
and conventional signaling pathway components are included in our revised
manuscript. For specific details, please refer to the discussion section (Page
17, Line 17-30; Page 18, Line 26 - Page 19, Line 14) and are presented below.

for primed hESC pluripotency, shares downstream branches such as MEK/ERK
and PI3K/AKT with the VEGF pathway. Given that both FGFR and MEK

only triggered trophoblast-like lineage specification but also led to cell death,

Comment 2: Below are the areas that I think are the most problematic in terms
of language and interpretation, as well as proposed solutions for making sure
this very interesting study is clearly communicated to the field.
In particular, the reported differentiation of primed state hESCs into bona fide
TSCs is still controversial, as this would represent a bona fide
transdifferentiation event that includes global rewiring of the epigenome. As
such, it would not conform with the developmental dynamics of the early
epiblast in vivo. Instead, BMP or CDX2 induction of primed state cells seems to
create a complex hybrid, possibly amniotic state that still fits many of the

(see in particular PMID: 33831365IF: 19.8 Q1 as well as PMID: 21816365IF:
19.8 Q1 ). My suggestion is that the authors consider the pre-existing literature
carefully when developing and explaining their model. To me, they must either
use the incorporated data and criteria from these previously papers to show
more completely that their cell types resemble more conventional hTSCs
compared to primed state derived amnion-like cells or they must substantially
revise this section of the manuscript to highlight these prior works. They must
make it clear that VEGF blocked primed state pluripotent cells from
32

Response to comment 2: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We
acknowledge that the issue of whether primed-state hESCs give rise to

inhibition of VEGF signaling disrupted self-renewal of primed hESCs severely,
leading to differentiation with the morphology and transcriptome similar to those
of the trophoblast lineage. The uniformly differentiated cells displayed a
morphology reminiscent of trophoblasts and expressed human TSC markers,
such as CDX2, TP63 and ELF5. Moreover, these cells could be induced to
express marker genes of ST and EVT cells. Therefore, we considered these
cells as TSC-like cells in the original manuscript. After reading your comments,
we realize that our characterization is not sufficient to claim that they are hTSC-
like cells. In fact, these cells lack a self-renewal capacity when they are cultured

the revised manuscript and do not claim them as TSCs in the revised
manuscript. Instead, in the revised manuscript, we consider that VEGF
signaling inhibition in primed hESCs could induce trophoblast-like
differentiation, based on the following experimental evidence: i) differentiated
cells derived from VEGFRi-treated hESCs displayed a uniform morphology
reminiscent of trophoblasts; ii) these cells exhibited lower levels of HLA-ABC,
which is expressed in amnion; iii) they expressed human TE and CT markers,
such as TROP2, GATA3, CDX2, TP63 and ELF5; iv) they had lower
methylation levels in the ELF5 promoter compared to undifferentiated hESCs;
v) they could be induced to express marker genes of ST and EVT cells. In
addition, a set of genes, including ACMSD, AQP9, CLDN22, TMEM174,
expressed in the amnion 9. We found that these genes were not upregulated in

also expressed in amnion cells. Moreover, there are differences in cell growth

vivo developmental environment. Therefore, we do not rule out the possibility

Collectively, we consider that the lineage specification limitation is not

It is likely that primed hESCs do not differentiate to trophoblast lineages, but to

Comment 3: The authors have done a convincing job of showing that VEGF

more similar to an “epistasis” test (establishing the genetic order of events) than
they are about direct or functional connections. The observation that NANOG
binds some BMP-associated effectors is interesting, but derived from previously
generated/public data and does not prove that NANOG is directly suppressing
these targets. The language (and subheader) related to the section “NANOG
directly suppresses expression of genes associated with the BMP pathway and
trophoblast lineage in primed hESCs” should be revised accordingly to better
utilize wording related to who is acting upstream to stabilize NANOG expression
(VEGF) or downstream to support spontaneous differentiation (BMP4). The
observation that NANOG appears to bind some of these promoters can be
noted and the authors can suggest that this might suggest that NANOG plays
dual activating and inhibitory roles, but anything beyond that is speculation not
present in the data.
Response to comment 3: Based on the following two results, we concluded
that NANOG is a major mediator downstream of VEGF signaling: 1) VEGF
signaling inhibition dramatically reduced NANOG expression; 2) NANOG OE
could largely rescue phenotypes induced by VEGF signaling deficiency.
However, these results do not indicate direct or indirect link between VEGF
signaling and NANOG. Yes, VEGF signaling is upstream of NANOG expression.
